text: Anselm Kiefer, born on 8 March 1945 in Donaueschingen, Germany, the son of a German art teacher, grew up in a city heavily bombed at the end of World War II, experiencing the war's devastation firsthand. His family moved to Ottersdorf in 1951, and he attended public school in Rastatt, graduating in 1965. He initially studied pre-law and Romance languages at the University of Freiburg before switching to art, studying at art academies in Freiburg and Karlsruhe, where he studied under Peter Dreher, a realist and figurative painter. He received an art degree in 1969. In 1971, Kiefer moved to Hornbach (Walldürn) and established a studio, remaining in the Neckar-Odenwald-Kreis until 1992, during which time his work is known as The German Years. In 1992, he relocated to France, first to Barjac, and from 2008 lived primarily in Paris in the Marais district with his second wife, the Austrian photographer Renate Graf, and their two children; they divorced in 2014. Kiefer has lived and worked in France since 1992, and since 2008 has resided primarily in Paris. In 2018, he was awarded Austrian citizenship. His works incorporate materials such as straw, ash, clay, lead, and shellac, and he values a "spiritual connection" with these materials, extracting the spirit already within them through processes like acid baths and physical blows with sticks and axes. He is particularly drawn to lead for its alchemical properties, noting its colorful appearance during heating and melting, especially the gold-like hues associated with alchemists. Straw represents energy due to its gold color and heat when burned, with the resulting ash symbolizing new creation and transformation. Kiefer emphasizes a balance between order and chaos, stating that too much order makes a piece dead and too much chaos prevents coherence, and he believes his works lose their power if placed in inappropriate spaces. His early career included performances documented in photographs titled Occupations and Heroische Sinnbilder, in which he dressed in his father's Wehrmacht uniform and mimicked the Nazi salute in France, Switzerland, and Italy to provoke German reflection on the Third Reich's xenophobia. In 1969, he presented his first solo exhibition, "Besetzungen (Occupations)," at Galerie am Kaiserplatz in Karlsruhe. His paintings have grown increasingly large, incorporating lead, broken glass, and dried plants, resulting in encrusted surfaces and thick impasto. By 1970, while studying informally under Joseph Beuys at Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, his style resembled Georg Baselitz’s, using glass, straw, wood, and plant parts, creating temporary, fragile works that emphasized natural forms. He returned to his birthplace in 1971 and later incorporated German mythology and studied Kabbalah, including the works of Robert Fludd. He made extended journeys throughout Europe, the US, and the Middle East, which influenced his work. In the 1970s and early 1980s, he created works based on Richard Wagner’s Der Ring des Nibelungen, and in the early 1980s produced over thirty paintings referencing Paul Celan’s poem "Todesfuge" ("Death Fugue"). Between 1980 and 1983, he painted looming stone edifices referencing National Socialist architecture, particularly buildings by Albert Speer and Wilhelm Kreis; the grand plaza in To the Unknown Painter (1983) specifically refers to the outdoor courtyard of Hitler’s Chancellery in Berlin. Between 1984 and 1985, he made works on paper with manipulated black-and-white photographs of desolate landscapes with utility poles and power lines, such as Heavy Cloud (1985), in response to West Germany’s controversy over NATO’s nuclear missile stationing. By the mid-1980s, his themes expanded to include art and culture’s fate, occult symbolism, theology, and mysticism, focusing on societal trauma and renewal. His 1980s paintings became more physical, featuring unusual textures and materials. He incorporated ancient Hebrew and Egyptian history, as in Osiris and Isis (1985–87), and in the 1990s shifted to universal myths of existence and meaning. From 1995 to 2001, he produced a cycle of large cosmic paintings. One of his most unusual works is 20 Years of Solitude (1971–1991), a ceiling-high stack of hundreds of white-painted ledgers and handmade books strewn with dirt and dried vegetation, with pages stained by his semen; the title references his frequent masturbation during its creation. He shocked the art world in May 1993 at a dinner party in New York, where he and Renate Graf decorated a candlelit loft with white muslin, skinned animals on hooks, white sand, and waiters dressed as mimes, serving arcane white organ meats, which guests found unappetizing; performers including Johanna Constantine, Lavinia Coop, Armen Ra, and Flotilla DeBarge were hired, and Anohni sang for the guests. Since 2002, he has worked with concrete, creating towers for Pirelli warehouses in Milan, paintings of the sea and boats with leaden objects (2004–05), rune motif paintings (2004–06), and other sculptures. In 2003, he held his first solo show at Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac, Salzburg Villa Katz, titled Am Anfang, focusing on history and myths. In 2005, he held a second exhibition, Für Paul Celan, at the same gallery, focusing on books and Germanic mythology linked to Paul Celan’s poetry, featuring eleven canvas works, bound books, and five sculptures, including a monumental outdoor concrete and lead sculpture, lead books with bronze sunflowers, lead ships and wedges, and two lead books from The Secret Life of Plants. The exhibition toured to Paris and Galerie Yvon Lambert. In 2006, his exhibition Velimir Chlebnikov was shown in a studio near Barjac, then at White Cube in London, and finally at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum in Connecticut; it consists of 30 large (2 × 3 meters) paintings in two banks of 15, hung in a corrugated steel building mimicking the studio, referencing the Russian futurist Velimir Chlebnikov’s theories of a "language of the future" called "Zaum" and cataclysmic sea battles every 317 years, with toy-like, battered, rusted battleships hanging in paint and plaster waves, using black, white, gray, and rust colors. In 2007, he became the first artist since Georges Braque in 1970 to be commissioned to install a permanent work at the Louvre, Paris, and inaugurated the Monumenta exhibitions series at the Grand Palais, honoring Paul Celan and Ingeborg Bachmann. In 2009, he mounted two exhibitions at White Cube in London: Karfunkelfee, a series of forest diptychs and triptychs in glass vitrines filled with Moroccan thorns, referencing a term from German Romanticism by Ingeborg Bachmann, and The Fertile Crescent, a group of epic paintings inspired by a trip to India, linking Mesopotamian civilizations to post-WWII German ruins, with historian Simon Schama noting its meditation on the instability of built grandeur. In Morgenthau Plan (2012), a golden wheat field sculpture is enclosed in a five-meter-high steel cage. That year, he inaugurated a gallery space in Pantin, with the exhibition Die Ungeborenen, accompanied by a publication with a letter by Kiefer and essays by Alexander Kluge and Emmanuel Daydé. He continues to be represented by Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac and participates in group and solo exhibitions at their locations. In 1969, Kiefer began designing books; early examples are worked-over photographs, while recent ones consist of lead sheets layered with paint, minerals, or dried plant matter, such as the lead books on steel shelves symbolizing stored, discarded historical knowledge. The book Rhine (1981) comprises 25 woodcuts suggesting a journey along the Rhine River, with scenes of the unspoiled river interrupted by dark, swirling pages representing the sinking of the battleship Bismarck in 1941 during an Atlantic sortie codenamed Rhine Exercise. Kiefer’s first large studio was in the attic of his home in Hornbach, later moved to a factory in Buchen, and in 1988 he transformed a former brick factory in Höpfingen into an extensive artwork with installations and sculptures. In 1991, after twenty years in the Odenwald, he traveled to India, Mexico, Japan, Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, and the United States. In 1992, he established himself in Barjac, France, where he transformed his 35-hectare studio compound La Ribaute into a Gesamtkunstwerk—a derelict silk factory now housing an extensive system of glass buildings, archives, installations, storerooms, subterranean chambers, and corridors. Sophie Fiennes filmed the studio complex in Barjac for her documentary Over Your Cities Grass Will Grow (2010), which captured both the environment and the artist at work, with one critic noting that the project spans acres, featuring miles of corridors, large studio spaces, landscape paintings, sculptures, and serpentine excavated labyrinths resembling stalagmites or termite mounds, with no clear boundary between work and finished product.

Anselm Kiefer established himself in Barjac, France, in 1992, transforming a derelict silk factory into a 35-hectare studio compound called La Ribaute, which functions as a Gesamtkunstwerk and serves as a commentary on industrialization. The studio features an extensive system of glass buildings, archives, installations, storerooms, and subterranean chambers and corridors. Sophie Fiennes filmed the studio for her 2010 documentary Over Your Cities Grass Will Grow, which captured both the environment and Kiefer at work; one critic described it as a monumental, evolving concept-art organism with miles of corridors, large studio spaces, landscape paintings, sculptures, and earthy, labyrinthine structures resembling stalagmites or termite mounds, where the finished product remains indistinct and in constant transformation. In 2008, Kiefer left Barjac and moved to Paris, relocating his work to a 35,000 sq ft warehouse in Croissy-Beaubourg, formerly the depository for the La Samaritaine department store, transported by a fleet of 110 lorries. His abandoned Barjac studio is now maintained by a caretaker and left uninhabited, quietly awaiting nature’s takeover, as the film’s title suggests. Kiefer returned to Barjac in the summer of 2019 to live and work there. In 1969, he held his first solo exhibition at Galerie am Kaiserplatz in Karlsruhe, and in 1980, along with Georg Baselitz, represented Germany at the Venice Biennale. In 1997, he exhibited at the Museo Correr in Venice with a one-man show focusing on paintings and books. Comprehensive solo exhibitions have been held at the Kunsthalle Düsseldorf (1984), Art Institute of Chicago (1987), Sezon Museum of Art in Tokyo (1993), Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin (1991), Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York (1998), Fondation Beyeler in Basel (2001), Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth (2005), Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington D.C. (2006), and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (2007). In 2007, the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao presented a major survey of his recent work, and in 2009, the Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibited Broken Flowers and Grass: Nature and Landscape in the Drawings of Anselm Kiefer. In 2007, Kiefer created a permanent site-specific installation at the Louvre with the triptych Athanor and sculptures Danae and Hortus Conclusus, becoming the first living artist to do so since Georges Braque in 1953. In 2008, he installed Palmsonntag (Palm Sunday) (2006) at the First Baptist Church of Los Angeles, reconfiguring the space with sanded floors and a new wall for the reliquary paintings, and later exhibited it at the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto with eight new panels. In 2010, he presented Next Year in Jerusalem at Gagosian Gallery, explaining that each work responded to a personal "shock" from recent news. In September 2013, The Hall Art Foundation, in partnership with MASS MoCA, opened a long-term installation in a 10,000 square-foot repurposed building, including Étroits sont les Vaisseaux (Narrow are the Vessels) (2002), The Women of the Revolution (Les Femmes de la Revolution) (1992), Velimir Chlebnikov (2004), and a new large-format lead photograph. In 2015, the Centre Pompidou, Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris, and Museum der bildenden Künste in Leipzig hosted a retrospective celebrating Kiefer’s 70th birthday. In 2016, the Albertina in Vienna held an exhibition of 35 woodcuts from 1977 to 2015. In 2017, the Met Breuer presented Provocations: Anselm Kiefer at The Met Breuer, spanning his career. In May 2018, Kiefer unveiled his first public art commission in the United States at Rockefeller Center, the Uraeus sculpture, inspired by Egyptian religious symbols and Thus Spoke Zarathustra, on view until 22 July. From October 18, 2025, to January 25, 2026, the Saint Louis Art Museum exhibited Anselm Kiefer: Becoming the Sea, a retrospective of his 60-year career, accompanied by a catalog. Kiefer received the Wolf Prize in 1990 and the Praemium Imperiale from the Japan Art Association in 1999, with the latter’s explanatory statement noting his complex engagement with history, his use of figures like Wagner and Goethe to address German cultural history, and his belief in art’s duty to confront the past and ethical questions, enabling the possibility of absolution through human effort. In 2008, he was awarded the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade, the first given to a visual artist, with art historian Werner Spies noting Kiefer’s passion for literature. In 2011, Kiefer was appointed chair of creativity in art at the Collège de France. Due to the spontaneous nature of his process, many of his works face stability concerns, which he acknowledges as part of the transformation process, a theme rooted in alchemy. He favors materials like lead for their alchemical properties—particularly its color shifts during heating, including gold, and its oxidation, which he accelerates with acid—and associates lead with the planet Saturn and magic numbers. Shellac is another favored material, valued for its color and energy, becoming warm when polished. Straw is used for its golden hue and energy, releasing heat and warmth when burned, symbolizing new creation and the cycle of life. The best-selling painting, The Fertile Crescent (2009), sold for $3,997,103 at China Guardian on June 3, 2019, surpassing the previous record of $3,554,500 for To the Unknown Painter (1983) sold at Christie's New York on May 11, 2011, and $3,549,350 for Let a Thousand Flowers Bloom (1999) sold at Christie's London on February 8, 2007. Kiefer’s works are held in public collections including the Hamburger Bahnhof, Berlin; Museum of Modern Art and Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York; Detroit Institute of Arts; Tate Modern, London; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto; North Carolina Museum of Art, Raleigh; High Museum of Art, Atlanta; Albright-Knox Art Gallery, Buffalo; Philadelphia Museum of Art; National Gallery of Australia, Canberra; Tel Aviv Museum of Art; and the Albertina, Vienna. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York owns 20 of his rare watercolors. Notable private collectors include Eli Broad and Andrew J. Hall.
